name: Zoe Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, governments or political parties. We don’t sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I supervise five returns administrators at a large sports-equipment company, and I'm still learning how to set priorities when everything arrives marked urgent. I'm 58, have a bachelor's degree in sports science, and ran swimming classes on my own before the pool lease ended; that didn't teach me corporate reporting or how to manage five adults. My partner is a part-time hospital porter, our children are grown, and our 27,000 savings cover five months of our 5,400 household spending, including rent and annual bills. I get typical management pay and use the approved AI summary tool occasionally after a colleague has shown me a reliable use; we'd planned for me to work until 70 to rebuild pension years, but payable dates and net amounts haven't been established.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people at work to keep the useful summary tool and stop waiting for it to solve a damaged bicycle claim by magic. We can save five minutes and still need to check what actually came back in the box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel reasonably secure because this looks like the ordinary work we've already budgeted around. My 4,600 take-home and my partner's 1,400 cover our 5,400 spending, leaving 600, and the 27,000 stays separate for trouble. There are some similar employers within reach if the company has an ordinary setback. I wouldn't feel obliged to turn myself into a different person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the twice-weekly returns review and use the approved summary tool for the cases we've already cleared for it. I'd continue asking my boss to check the weekly priorities in the existing paid review, because the tool doesn't decide what my team should do first. We'd keep transferring the existing 600 monthly into savings while both wages lasted, and I'd leave the first year without a new course purchase or business launch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and glad to put the worry back at its normal size. I can enjoy learning a job without needing to call it a reinvention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the returns review worth doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A buyer might say a machine is faulty when the wrong attachment was supplied. We look at the actual return and paperwork before deciding whether to refund or send the missing part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you reopen swimming classes in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't have a pool contract or paying pupils waiting. I can miss the old work without pretending it is income available today.

say: I'd keep the **useful summary tool** without expecting magic answers to damaged-product claims.
I'd insist we check **what was returned** even when software saves a few minutes.
think: I feel **reasonably secure** because two wages cover our budget and the reserve remains separate.
Some **local alternatives** offer options after an ordinary company setback, without requiring me to become a different person.
do: Keep **returns reviews** and approved summary uses, with priorities checked in the existing paid meeting.
Continue the existing **600 monthly saving** while both wages last, without purchasing a course or launching a business.
feel: **Calm**, able to enjoy learning the job without calling it a reinvention.
S0.quote: I can enjoy learning a job without needing to call it a reinvention.
fieldNote: Her **calm** rests on both current incomes, a separate reserve and some local alternatives rather than automatic comfort from her age.
She separates **missing swimming work** from having an available pool, pupils or income, avoiding an assumed self-employment fallback.

steps.text: Continue returns reviews, approved summaries and the existing paid priority check
Continue the existing 600 monthly savings transfer while both wages last

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say returns checking and customer answers are exactly the work the company could automate. I'd want a demonstration we can question, rather than a room of people pretending they already understand it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own post could shrink because reporting, checking and allocating cases are most of what I do, and I'm not especially good at the allocation yet. Learning the tool might help me do this job while it lasts; it wouldn't establish that the company needs the same number of managers. I could cope with a search using our reserve, but I wouldn't be comfortable losing the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my boss to approve two paid two-hour sessions with the colleague who already uses the company's returns tool well. I'd start only after the hours and the colleague's time were agreed in writing, using cleared training cases, no personal fees and no assumed unpaid catch-up. In the first year I'd apply the demonstrated checks only within our existing approval rules, continuing the current process if training wasn't approved. At home I'd cancel the 80 monthly sports package and 70 meal subscription, putting the extra 150 with our usual 600 into savings only while both wages and other costs held.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I work better when somebody shows me a real case and lets me ask the obvious question. I'd rather be the learner who stops the demonstration than the manager who nods through a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask during the demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which fields came from the actual return and which were inferred, because a confident description can hide a missing serial number. I'd ask the colleague to show me the original record before I'd use the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the 750 saving assume the employer pays for the sessions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the learning request is for existing paid hours with no personal fee. If it wasn't approved I'd continue the old process, not quietly buy training and still tell my partner we were saving 750.

say: I'd identify **returns checking and answers** as directly exposed rather than pretend managers stand outside the change.
I'd want a **demonstration open to questions** where staff can stop and ask what they don't understand.
think: My **own post** could shrink because checking, reporting and allocating cases dominate it, and my allocation skill is still weak.
Learning helps only **while work lasts**, while our reserve makes a search possible without making wage loss comfortable.
do: Request **four paid training hours**; start only with written time and colleague approval, cleared cases, no fees and no assumed unpaid catch-up.
Apply demonstrated checks within **existing rules** if approved; otherwise continue the current process.
Cancel **150 monthly** in sports and meal subscriptions, raising saving to 750 only while both wages and other costs hold.
feel: **Anxious but teachable**, preferring obvious questions to nodding through a mistake.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the learner who stops the demonstration than the manager who nods through a mistake.
fieldNote: Her **learning** follows a proven colleague, with explicit approval, paid time, record and fee conditions before starting.
The **750 saving** combines an actual subscription cut with existing saving and depends on continued wages and unchanged other costs.

steps.text: Request four approved paid training hours with cleared cases and no personal fees
Cancel the sports package and meal subscription totalling 150 monthly
Save 750 monthly only while both wages and other costs hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children the returns desk could go before a robot can carry a damaged treadmill. I'd rather look at real vacancies further away than assume a familiar local title protects the same thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty in 2028 and expect my management wage to disappear, with no confirmed pension available then. My partner's 1,400 leaves 4,000 of today's monthly costs uncovered; the 27,000 reserve would carry that gap for less than seven months, not the decade to our planned finish. His physical porter work might last longer, but the 2031 robots mean it isn't a permanent guarantee. I'd lose sleep over spending the reserve merely waiting for the old job to return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply now for actual returns or administration vacancies in the larger town where our son lives, without asking him to promise us accommodation. I'd accept only signed employment terms and a fully costed household plan leaving at least 300 monthly after new housing and travel, counting my partner's wage as zero unless his continued or replacement work was confirmed. We'd move only with an agreed lease, both partners' agreement, and deposits plus moving costs capped at 3,500 from the reserve, leaving at least 23,500 accessible; I'd assume no free interview travel or paid leave without written approval. In the first year after AGI I'd keep looking if no offer met those conditions and request only eligible support after wage loss, without treating another thinking job as safe from AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, with a need to do something more concrete than reading job forecasts. I'd rather price a real bus journey than picture a perfect job in a town I've never visited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move first and find work afterward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not under this plan; the employment terms and budget come first, then a lease and funded move. Our son has his own household, and proximity isn't an offer to live in his spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the only offer leaves 100 after costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't meet the 300 margin I've set, so we'd have to decline or separately agree a genuinely revised funded plan. I wouldn't erase the margin just because I was relieved somebody had replied.

say: I'd explain that **returns thinking work** can disappear before robots carry returned equipment.
I'd look further away rather than trust a **familiar local title** to protect the same tasks.
think: At **sixty**, I expect salary loss without confirmed pension access and a 4,000 monthly gap after my partner's wage.
Our **reserve** covers that gap for under seven months, while his porter income faces later robots and waiting would cost sleep.
do: Apply in my **son's town**; accept only signed terms and a costed plan leaving 300 monthly after housing/travel, excluding unconfirmed partner wages.
Move only with **agreed lease and partnership**, costs at most 3,500 and at least 23,500 accessible; assume no unapproved interview funding.
Continue seeking actual **vacancies** if those gates fail and request only eligible support after wage loss.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, wanting real costs and offers rather than forecasts.
S2.quote: I'd rather price a real bus journey than picture a perfect job in a town I've never visited.
fieldNote: Her **relocation** separates applications, signed work, budget, housing and household agreement, without assuming her partner's wage transfers or her son provides space.
The **move cap** protects a stated cash minimum, and she gives neither interview costs nor another office job guaranteed funding or security.

steps.text: Apply for actual returns or administration vacancies in her son’s town
Accept signed work only under the 300 monthly margin and confirmed-income household gate
Move only with agreed lease, shared agreement and the 3,500 cost/23,500 cash gates
Request eligible support after wage loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to work out whether fewer hours could actually work, instead of announcing a retirement we can't afford. I'd rather ask for a small change clearly than leave my team to guess whether I'm half leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 in 2031 and expect the returns role to go even if I became much better at it. Before that, I'd like some weekday time with our granddaughter, but I can't buy it by pretending a lower wage costs nothing. My partner's work and a possible pension don't turn five years into guaranteed retirement funding, especially with robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the employer for a written quote for a nine-day fortnight from age 62, with actual duties, hours, take-home pay and pension deductions, not start taking alternate Fridays off. I'd agree only if confirmed household take-home after work travel stayed at least 5,600 against our current 5,400 costs, my partner agreed, and the employer approved the schedule in writing; otherwise I'd keep current hours. Any grandchild care would need her parents' agreement and a check that our health and travel made it workable, with no childcare wage assumed. I'd obtain actual pension dates and net figures now, and in the first year after AGI I'd seek paid vacancies and eligible support if the role ended rather than assume shorter hours had protected it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the main wage ending, though the extra preparation makes me less likely to grab the first suggestion. A day with my granddaughter is worth asking for, not worth hiding the cost of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a nine-day fortnight necessarily meet 5,600?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't know the employer's actual net-pay figure, and it might fail the test. That's why it's a request for a quote, not a signed change or an arrangement I've promised my granddaughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you fund the missing amount from savings if it failed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not under this plan; that would turn a recurring wage reduction into a countdown in the cash account. We'd keep the existing hours and find another way to see the family.

say: I'd ask whether **shorter hours** work financially rather than announce unaffordable retirement.
I'd discuss a **clear schedule change** rather than leave colleagues guessing whether I'm leaving.
think: At **63**, I expect the returns role to go even if my management skills improve.
I want **granddaughter time** before then, but neither a lower wage nor unconfirmed pension creates free retirement funding.
do: Request a **nine-day-fortnight quote** from age 62 with actual duties, hours, net pay and pension deductions.
Agree only with **written employer approval**, partner agreement and confirmed household net after travel of 5,600 minimum; otherwise keep current hours.
Arrange **unpaid grandchild care** with parental agreement and health/travel checks; obtain pension figures, seek vacancies and eligible support after job loss.
feel: **Alarmed but less rushed**, unwilling to hide the recurring cost of family time.
S3.quote: A day with my granddaughter is worth asking for, not worth hiding the cost of.
fieldNote: Her **hours request** is not permission to change the schedule, and she explicitly rejects filling a failed recurring budget with savings.
The **childcare plan** has household, parental, health and travel gates and carries no assumed wage or guarantee against later job loss.

steps.text: Request nine-day-fortnight terms; agree after written employer approval, partner agreement and ≥5,600 household net after travel
Keep existing hours if the quote or household conditions fail
Seek actual paid vacancies if the returns job ends
Request eligible support after job loss if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to consider a different finish, not a guarantee that everybody can afford one. I'd want to leave the team a clear handover rather than spend two years pretending a vanished job was coming back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 in 2036, two years before our existing plan for me to finish at 70, and I'd expect this job to go then. I'd be less frightened if I could fund those years by changing the retirement plan rather than finding another desk, but the pension access and amounts are still unknown. My partner's porter wage could face robots around 2039, so I'd need a plan that didn't quietly require him to work forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my planning target from 70 to 68 and request written pension access dates, net amounts, deductions and any earlier-draw penalty now. I wouldn't give notice until confirmed household retirement income covered actual costs plus an allowance for unexpected bills without depending on either unconfirmed wage; if it failed, the earlier target wouldn't become a departure. I'd ask a community pension service for help interpreting the figures only after confirming the appointment had no fee, and review them annually with my partner. In the first year after AGI we'd use the actual agreed income plan if affordable retirement had become possible, or seek paid work and eligible support if it hadn't, without treating age 68 itself as entitlement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a little relieved to give the end of work a proper test instead of insisting on 70 whatever happened. Moving a date in my notebook is easy; earning the right to stop is the part I still have to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has actually changed in the retirement plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The target I've written down would be 68 rather than the 70 we'd been using. The funding test hasn't been passed, so I wouldn't tell payroll or the family that my last day was agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a pension estimate be enough to give notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd need written eligibility and the actual net amounts we'd be entitled to, checked against the budget. I'd also want to understand what changed if either of us died, rather than assume one household figure lasted unchanged forever.

say: I'd consider a **different finish** while recognising that ten years doesn't guarantee affordability.
I'd want a **clear handover** instead of waiting for a vanished role to return.
think: At **68**, I expect job loss two years before our existing plan to finish at 70.
Earlier retirement might ease fear, but **pension access** is unknown and my partner's wage cannot be assumed forever.
do: Move my **planning target** from 70 to 68 and obtain written pension dates, net amounts, deductions and earlier-draw penalties.
Give notice only after **confirmed retirement income** covers actual costs and unexpected bills without uncertain wages, including understanding survivor-income changes.
Use **community pension help** only after confirming no fee, review annually and seek work or eligible support if affordable retirement isn't established.
feel: **Anxious but slightly relieved**, testing an earlier finish rather than insisting on 70.
S4.quote: Moving a date in my notebook is easy; earning the right to stop is the part I still have to check.
fieldNote: Her **earlier target** explicitly advances an existing age-70 plan to 68, while departure still requires confirmed affordable income.
The **funding test** includes eligibility, net amounts, penalties and survivor changes, with no fee assumed for the requested community appointment.

steps.text: Bring the existing retirement target from 70 to 68, departing only after confirmed affordable funding
Request no-fee community help interpreting written pension and survivor-income terms
Seek paid vacancies if the earlier retirement funding test fails after job loss

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be sixty with a long stretch before our planned finish, and the main wage could go at once. I'd want real notice, paid access to employer-approved learning, and pension advice that explained actual ages and net amounts rather than calling me nearly retired. I can still earn my way if somebody has work to offer; I can't accept a vacancy that exists only in a speech.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a late move into management means someone has chosen a grand new career or just found a regular wage after a lease ended. I miss teaching children to swim, but that doesn't make opening another class a funded plan. My partner and I would rather make a modest choice together than tell the children we'd solved everything.

headlineQuote: I can still earn my way if somebody has work to offer; I can't accept a vacancy that exists only in a speech.
portrait: Zoe is **58**, a junior returns manager with a sports-science bachelor's degree who still struggles with priorities and corporate reporting.
Her **swimming classes ended** when the pool lease ended; she now values the regular wage and uses proven AI tools occasionally.
She and her **hospital-porter partner** have grown children and five months of household expenses saved, with some similar employers locally.
Her existing **work-until-70 plan** meets different choices across the scenarios, including gated relocation, shorter hours and a conditional earlier retirement target.
biggestWorry: I fear **AGI by 2028** most because a main-wage loss at sixty leaves a long stretch before our planned finish.
whatWouldHelp: I need **real notice**, paid approved learning and advice establishing actual pension ages and net amounts.
